title: fix(process): fail wait4 stores with EFAULT like Linux
body:
Fixes #220

## Summary

- The managed `wait4` stored the status word and the zeroed `rusage` with `PTRACE_POKETEXT`. A ptrace write ignores page protections, so a status pointer into read-only memory was written where Linux returns `-EFAULT`. An unmapped status or `rusage` pointer made the store fail, and the supervisor failed the domain.
- Both stores now go through the new `write_tracee_bytes` in `supervisor.rs`, a `process_vm_writev` of the whole buffer that honors the tracee's page protections. A short write counts as `-EFAULT`.
- Kernels built without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH` return `ENOSYS` for `process_vm_writev` (for example minimal VM guest kernels), and a custom seccomp profile can return `EPERM`. If the first call fails with `ENOSYS`, `EPERM` or `EACCES`, the helper caches that and from then on uses the previous `PTRACE_PEEKDATA`/`PTRACE_POKEDATA` writes. A failed access (`EIO` or `EFAULT`) becomes `-EFAULT`, and `ESRCH` stays `ESRCH`. This path has reduced fidelity: an unmapped buffer still gives `-EFAULT`, but read-only memory is written, as before this change. The switch is announced once with `GINUX_SUPERVISOR_AUDIT: tracee-write=ptrace-fallback process_vm_writev=-38` (or `-1`).
- A store that faults makes `wait4` return `-EFAULT` to the caller, on the direct path and on the wakeup of a parked waiter. As in `kernel_wait4`, the child stays reaped, the status is stored before the `rusage`, and a faulting status skips the `rusage`. A new audit line `wait store fault caller=N reaped=M` records it.
- A status word that crosses a page boundary is written all or nothing, like the kernel's single 4-byte store. The part on the second page goes first; if the first page then faults, the second part gets its previous bytes back. A faulting `rusage` keeps the bytes before the fault, as `copy_to_user` does (measured natively).
- Any error other than `EFAULT` (for example `ESRCH` for a tracee that is gone) keeps the existing killed-task check and domain failure. A tracee killed during the store is still caught by the `PTRACE_SETREGS`/`PTRACE_SYSCALL` that follows.
- An unaligned `rusage` buffer no longer fails the domain. Linux accepts it, and so does `process_vm_writev`.
- The parent-tid store of `clone` (`store_tracee_tid`) keeps its unchecked ptrace write, now through the shared byte-merge helper `poke_tracee_bytes` (same per-word merge as before). The kernel ignores a failed `CLONE_PARENT_SETTID` store, so making it honor protections needs its own change.

Details and reproduction: #220.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-init/src/supervisor.rs`: `write_tracee_bytes` with the cached ptrace fallback, `poke_tracee_bytes`, `fault_errno`, `syscall6`, `SYS_PROCESS_VM_WRITEV`, `EIO`, `EACCES`, `EFAULT`.
- `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`: `store_wait_results` (status, then `rusage`) and `store_tracee_status` (all-or-nothing status word) replace the ptrace stores. Both `wait4` store sites return `-EFAULT` on a fault. `store_tracee_tid` calls `poke_tracee_bytes`.
- `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c`: scenarios `ro_status`, `bad_status`, `bad_rusage` and `straddle_status`. Each one reaps a child twice, once after it exited (`WNOHANG` poll) and once from a parked wait, and prints the result, the read-only word, the bytes around the faulting buffers, the status, the first `rusage` word and a second `wait4`.
- `scripts/test-process-native.py`: expected lines for these scenarios, the same as natively, with 20 repetitions each. A check that both rounds faulted and the second one parked, so both store sites are covered. New modes `<scenario>/vm-writev-enosys` and `<scenario>/vm-writev-eperm` for `wait_status`, `ro_status`, `bad_status` and `bad_rusage` run the same fixtures with a seccomp filter (installed with `ctypes`, no root needed) that fails `process_vm_writev` with `ENOSYS` or `EPERM`. They expect the fallback audit line, the same lines for `wait_status`, `bad_status` and `bad_rusage`, and the reduced-fidelity result for `ro_status` (the wait succeeds and the read-only word is written). The wrapped modes must report the fallback. In a plain mode the supervisor's own audit line decides which result applies: where it reports the fallback, for example on a kernel without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, `ro_status` expects the reduced-fidelity result. `straddle_status` has no fallback mode: the page after its status word is unmapped, so the store already faults at the `PTRACE_PEEKTEXT` of that page, before any write.
- `Makefile`: the four scenarios added to `build-process-fixtures`.

## Testing

The four scenarios fail on `main`'s binary (64a3e3f7): `ro_status` with `wait=2` and `ro cell=10752` (the read-only word was written), the other three with a domain failure (`wait status store failed` or `wait rusage store failed`). With this change all four pass 20 of 20 runs in each of two full runs.

With `process_vm_writev` failing with `ENOSYS`, as on a kernel without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, a first version of this change without the fallback failed `wait_status` with `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait result store failed`. `main` passes there, because it only uses ptrace. With the fallback, the eight `/vm-writev-*` modes pass. The whole `make test-process-native` also passes when run under an `ENOSYS` filter and under an `EPERM` filter. In 200 further direct runs (50 per scenario, half of them pinned to one CPU) the blocking round parked every time.

| case | Linux (pid namespace) | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| status in `.rodata` (`ro_status`) | `-14`, word untouched, `rusage` untouched | child pid, word = `10752` | `-14`, word untouched, `rusage` untouched |
| status unmapped (`bad_status`) | `-14`, then `ECHILD` | domain failure | `-14`, then `ECHILD` |
| `rusage` unmapped (`bad_rusage`) | `-14`, status `10752` stored | domain failure | `-14`, status `10752` stored |
| status crossing into an unmapped page (`straddle_status`) | `-14`, both bytes untouched | domain failure | `-14`, both bytes untouched |
| status crossing from `.rodata` into the writable page (manual probe) | `-14`, bytes on the writable page untouched | child pid, bytes on the writable page overwritten | `-14`, bytes on the writable page untouched |
| unaligned `rusage` (manual probe) | child pid, status stored | domain failure | child pid, status stored |
| kernel, wrapping and vsyscall addresses as status (manual probe) | `-14`, then `ECHILD` | not run | `-14`, then `ECHILD` |
| `ro_status` with `process_vm_writev` unavailable (fallback) | as above | child pid, word = `10752` | child pid, word = `10752` (reduced fidelity, as `main`) |
| the three manual probes above, fallback | as above | not run | `.rodata` crossing: child pid, both pages written (as `main`); unaligned `rusage`: as Linux; kernel addresses: as Linux |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build` | pass |
| `make test-process-native` (all scenarios incl. the four new ones, the eight `/vm-writev-*` modes and `legacy`), twice | pass |
| `make test-process-native` with `process_vm_writev` failing for the whole run, once with `ENOSYS`, once with `EPERM` | pass |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

title: process: wait4 status and rusage stores ignore page protections (no EFAULT)
body:
## Summary

In `ginux process-native`, a managed `wait4` that reaps a child stores the status word and the zeroed `rusage` into the caller with `PTRACE_PEEKTEXT`/`PTRACE_POKETEXT` (`store_tracee_status` and `zero_tracee_rusage` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`, called from arm `61` of `supervise_process_native` and from `wake_waiters_for_child`). A ptrace write ignores page protections, and a failed one is treated as a supervision failure. Both differ from Linux, where `kernel_wait4` stores the status with `put_user` and `wait4` copies the `rusage` with `copy_to_user`, and a fault returns `-EFAULT` after the child is reaped:

- A status pointer into read-only memory is written: `wait4` returns the child pid and the read-only word now holds the status. Linux returns `-EFAULT` and leaves the memory untouched.
- An unmapped status or `rusage` pointer makes the ptrace store fail, and the supervisor fails the whole domain (`GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, or `wait rusage store failed`). Linux returns `-EFAULT` to the caller, and the domain keeps running.
- The same holds for a status word that crosses from a writable page into an unmapped one; Linux writes none of its bytes. An unaligned `rusage` buffer also fails the domain, while Linux accepts it.

Both store sites behave the same: the direct one (the child had already exited, also with `WNOHANG`) and the wakeup of a parked waiter.

glibc's `wait4`/`waitpid` pass the kernel result through, so a program sees `-1` with `errno == EFAULT` on Linux. Under `process-native` it either gets a success with read-only memory changed or never returns, because the domain is torn down.

## Expected

As on Linux: `wait4` returns `-EFAULT`, the child stays reaped (a second `wait4` for it returns `-ECHILD`), and memory the caller cannot write stays untouched. The status is stored before the `rusage`, so a valid status with a faulting `rusage` is still written, and a faulting status skips the `rusage`.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds the scenarios `ro_status`, `bad_status`, `bad_rusage` and `straddle_status` to `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c` and `scripts/test-process-native.py`. Each one forks a child that exits with 42 and reaps it twice: first with a `WNOHANG` poll (the child has already exited), then with a blocking wait that parks while the child is still running. Each round passes these pointers:

| scenario | status pointer | rusage pointer |
|---|---|---|
| `ro_status` | an `int` in `.rodata` (read-only segment) | valid buffer |
| `bad_status` | `0x1000` (never mapped) | valid buffer |
| `bad_rusage` | valid `int` | `0x1000` |
| `straddle_status` | the last 2 bytes of the bss page, followed by an unmapped page | valid buffer |

The fixtures are static and `-nostdlib`, so they also run unchanged on Linux. Natively, in a new pid namespace (`unshare -Upfr --kill-child`), all four print `wait=-14` in both rounds, then `rewait=-10`, with the read-only word, the bytes around the faulting buffers and the skipped `rusage` untouched. In `bad_rusage` the status is still stored (`status=10752`).

With the PR checked out and `main`'s binary (64a3e3f7) built in a separate tree:

```
make build build-process-fixtures
python3 scripts/test-process-native.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/process target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/process-native-fixture ro_status
```

All four scenarios fail on `main`:

| scenario | `main` | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| `ro_status` | `nohang wait=2`, `nohang ro cell=10752` (same in the blocking round), exit 0 | `wait=-14`, `ro cell=0` |
| `bad_status` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, then `rewait=-10` |
| `bad_rusage` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait rusage store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, `status=10752`, then `rewait=-10` |
| `straddle_status` | `GINUX_DOMAIN: failed reason=wait status store failed`, exit 1 | `wait=-14`, `edge=30583` (both bytes untouched) |

Output of `ro_status` on `main` (host pids elided, blocking round shortened):

```
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: fork variant=fork host-result=... virtual-result=2
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: sigchld queued parent=1 child=2
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: sigchld delivered parent=1
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait selector=2 virtual-result=2 status=42
nohang wait=2
nohang ro cell=10752
...
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait parked caller=1 selector=3
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait wakeup caller=1 child=3 status=42
...
blocking wait=3
blocking ro cell=10752
```

## Suggested fix

- Write both buffers with `process_vm_writev`, which honors the tracee's page protections the way the kernel's own copy to user memory does, and return `-EFAULT` to the caller when a store faults. Where `process_vm_writev` is unavailable (`ENOSYS` on kernels built without `CONFIG_CROSS_MEMORY_ATTACH`, or `EPERM` from a custom seccomp profile), fall back to the ptrace writes and at least return `-EFAULT` for unmapped buffers. The child stays reaped, as on Linux. Keep the existing killed-task and domain-failure handling for any other error.
- Keep the kernel's order: status first, then `rusage`, and skip the `rusage` when the status store faults. Make the 4-byte status store all or nothing when it crosses a page boundary.

A PR follows.

title: launch/native: sysinfo exposes host uptime, load, memory and process count (deny or emulate?)
body:
## Summary

In `ginux launch` and `ginux native`, `sysinfo` (99) is in the balanced task surface (`balanced_surface` in `crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`), so `decide_balanced` mediates it and it executes on the host. The workload receives the host's `struct sysinfo` unchanged: uptime, the three load averages, total, free, shared and buffer RAM, total and free swap, and the host-wide process count.

None of these values belong to the domain. The configuration of both lanes (`config/domain-gate5.toml`) sets `vcpus = 1` and `memory_mib = 256`, but `totalram` is the host's physical memory and `procs` counts every task on the host. This is host-topology information admitted for compatibility only.

`ginux process-native` does not pass it through: 99 is not in its contract, so `supervise_process_native` fails it with `-ENOSYS` before it executes, like every other entry it does not list.

Fixing this changes observable behaviour in either direction, so I would like your decision on the policy before opening a PR.

## Reproduction

A freestanding probe that calls `sysinfo` on a pattern-filled buffer and prints the fields, run under `main` (2489517e) in both lanes, as root:

```
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=1 phase=entry syscall=99 action=mediate surface=task result=pending
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=1 phase=exit result=0
sysinfo=0
uptime=<host uptime in seconds>
load1=<host load> load5=<host load> load15=<host load>
totalram=<host MemTotal> freeram=<host MemFree>
totalswap=<host SwapTotal> freeswap=<host SwapFree>
procs=<host process count>
```

The values are consistent with `/proc/uptime`, `/proc/loadavg` (the loads are scaled by 65536) and `/proc/meminfo` read on the host at the same time; `totalram` equals `MemTotal` in bytes. `launch` shows the same with `ginux: audit ... syscall=99 action=mediate surface=task`. Under `process-native` the probe gets `sysinfo=-38` and its buffer keeps the pattern.

An ordinary dynamically linked glibc program sees the same: `sysinfo()` succeeds with the host values, and `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)`, which glibc derives from `sysinfo`, report the host's physical and available memory.

## Options

### A. Deny with `-ENOSYS`, as `process-native` does

Remove 99 from the task surface; `balanced_surface` then classifies it as `Denied`.

Consequence: glibc's `__get_phys_pages` and `__get_avphys_pages` ignore the `sysinfo` error and compute from the uninitialized `struct sysinfo` on the stack. `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` then return whatever the stack held, with `errno` `ENOSYS`. A probe that fills the stack with a byte before each call gave, in both lanes and with a current glibc (glibc 2.39 of Rocky 10 behaves the same way):

| stack fill | `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` | `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` |
|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `0` | `0` |
| `0x11` | `6148914691236512545` | `6148914691236512545` |
| `0x7f` | `-8897841259083690871` | `-8897841259083690871` |

Python's `os.sysconf` gave values like `0` and `7752550405618130944` in the same setting. Programs that size buffers or caches from physical memory then see an arbitrary, possibly huge or negative, value. `process-native` returns the same `-ENOSYS` today, so glibc there takes the same path. With the Rocky userland, coreutils `sort` (which calls `sysinfo`) still produces the same output; `nproc`, `ls`, `gawk`, `find`, `du`, `tail` and `bash` do not call it.

### B. Emulate a successful `sysinfo` with deterministic values

`sysinfo` moves to the virtual-identity surface and never executes on the host. The supervisor writes a fixed `struct sysinfo` into the task's buffer and returns 0. Two variants:

- **Zero-filled**: every counter 0, `mem_unit = 1`. `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` and `sysconf(_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES)` return 0 with `errno` 0, the same in every run. This follows the rule `process-native` already applies to `wait4`'s `rusage` ("without usage accounting the honest bounded content is zeros").
- **Domain values**: `totalram` from `memory_mib`, zero loads, `procs = 1`, uptime since the domain start, no swap. This keeps `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` meaningful, but the README states that this path "does not implement resource quotas from the domain metadata", so a workload would be told about a limit that is not enforced.

With the zero-filled variant the measured results are:

| check in `launch` and `native` | `main` | B (zero-filled) |
|---|---|---|
| audit | `action=mediate surface=task` | `action=emulate surface=virtual-identity result=0` |
| `sysinfo(&buffer)` | `0`, `<host values>` | `0`, all counters 0, `mem_unit` 1 |
| `sysinfo(NULL)`, `sysinfo(<read-only buffer>)` | `-14`, `-14` | `-14`, `-14` (buffer unchanged) |
| `sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES)` / `_SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` with the three stack fills | `<host pages>` | `0` / `0`, `errno` 0 |
| Rocky Bash native shell check | pass, no `sysinfo` call | pass, same audited sequence |

The buffer is written with `process_vm_writev`, which honors the task's page protections, so an unmapped or read-only buffer fails with `-EFAULT` as on Linux.

### Recommendation

I recommend B with the zero-filled struct: it is deterministic, it follows "virtualize, don't pass through" from #179, and it does not report an unenforced memory limit. A keeps today's `process-native` rule but leaves glibc's memory queries undefined. Either way the choice is yours. `process-native` would stay on `-ENOSYS` until you decide whether it should follow; I have kept it out of both variants.

## Scope

Other host-topology reads remain and are a separate question: `rseq` (334) registration makes the kernel write the host CPU number into the task's `rseq` area in all three lanes, and the same number is readable without any syscall through `rdtscp` and the vDSO `getcpu`, which ptrace cannot intercept.

Both variants are prepared with launch/native fixtures; I'll open the PR for whichever is chosen.

title: fix(vfs): resolve symlinks before parent path components
body:
With `/bin` pointing to `usr/bin`, VFS lookup currently resolves `/bin/..` to `/` instead of `/usr` because it normalizes parent components first. Resolve components in order for indexed lookup, open/create and unlink, checking intermediate directories and preserving the final link entry during unlink.

Standalone on `main`. Validation: `make check`, `make test-unit` (56 tests), the workflow's launch/native/process/setup checks, and the VFS CLI pass locally on Linux. The full Rocky VM suite was not rerun.

title: fix(vfs): retain unlinked files until their last close
body:
Unlink currently discards bytes still held by open VFS descriptors, while deleted entries permanently consume overlay slots. Preserve open objects, give recreated names independent contents, and reclaim unused slots while retaining image whiteouts, including paths through symlinked directories.

Standalone on `main`. Validation: `make check`, `make test-unit` (59 tests), the workflow's launch/native/process/setup checks, and the VFS CLI pass locally on Linux. The full Rocky VM suite was not rerun.

performed_via_github_app.name: ChatGPT Codex Connector
performed_via_github_app.description: Bring ChatGPT and Codex to your GitHub repositories.

title: fix(vfs): preserve files when open fails
body:
A failed VFS open can currently create an overlay file, copy up an image file, or truncate existing contents before returning `DescriptorLimit`. Reserve descriptor capacity before mutation, reject truncation without write authority, and discard incomplete copy-up after an image read fails.

Standalone on `main`. Validation: `make check`, `make test-unit` (58 tests), the workflow's launch/native/process/setup checks, and the VFS CLI pass locally on Linux. The full Rocky VM suite was not rerun.

title: fix(init): hide the host tid from set_tid_address and PI futexes
body:
Fixes #214

## Summary

This brings `ginux launch` and `ginux native` to the contract `process-native` already has (`crates/ginux-init/src/process_hooks.rs`: "PI operations are denied because they expose host tids"; `set_tid_address` is already translated there). No surface is admitted.

- `set_tid_address` stays mediated for its clear-on-exit registration, but its result, the caller's host tid, reached the workload next to the virtual pid 4242 from `getpid`. The exit stop now reports `BALANCED_VIRTUAL_PID` (4242) instead. Both lanes run one task without threads (`clone` and `fork` are denied), so its tid is its pid. The host keeps the registration, so the clear-on-exit write still happens; it stores 0, not a tid.
- `FUTEX_LOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_LOCK_PI2` and `FUTEX_TRYLOCK_PI` stored the caller's host tid in the futex word, and `FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI` and the requeue-PI operations compare the word against it. `balanced_arguments_allowed` now rejects these six operations, so both lanes deny them through their existing argument check with `-1` (`EPERM`), as they deny mutating opens. The command is classified by the low 7 bits of the operation word, the same mask `process-native` uses, so any combination of flag bits is covered, including the additional flag bits newer kernels accept (the fixture checks one, 1024). Every other futex operation stays mediated.
- `-1` rather than `-ENOSYS` is deliberate: glibc probes PI support with `FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI` and treats only `-ENOSYS` as missing support, so `pthread_mutex_init` with `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` would then fail with `ENOTSUP`. With `-1` it keeps succeeding (see the glibc probe below).
- Consequence: glibc stores the `set_tid_address` result as the thread's own tid, so a robust mutex taken by the workload now carries 4242 as owner, and the kernel's exit-time robust-list walk, which compares the owner with the host tid, no longer marks such a mutex `FUTEX_OWNER_DIED`. Only another task sharing the memory could observe that, and these lanes cannot create one.
- `gettid` stays `-ENOSYS` in these lanes; admitting it is a separate policy change.

If you prefer to decide the PI-futex rule separately, I can split that part into its own PR.

Details and reproduction: #214.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`: `SYS_FUTEX`, `SYS_SET_TID_ADDRESS`, `BALANCED_VIRTUAL_PID` (now also used by `balanced_identity_result`), `balanced_mediated_result` (the result reported for a mediated call whose host result is the caller's tid), `futex_priority_inheritance`, the `SYS_FUTEX` arm of `balanced_arguments_allowed`; unit tests `balanced_contract_reports_the_virtual_tid` and `balanced_contract_rejects_priority_inheritance_futexes` (all six PI commands rejected with `FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG`, `FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME`, 512, 1024, `1 << 20` and upper register bits; the other commands, including unknown ones, still mediated).
- `crates/ginux-init/src/launch.rs`, `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs` (`supervise_native`): the `Action::Mediate` arm overrides the exit result when `balanced_mediated_result` names one.
- `tests/fixtures/launch-fixture.c`, `tests/fixtures/native-fixture.c`: scenario `virtual-tid` (prints `set_tid_address`, `getpid`, `gettid`, and the `FUTEX_LOCK_PI` results and futex words without and with flag bit 1024); `native-fixture.c` gains a `call4` helper for the `r10` argument.
- `scripts/test-launch.py`, `scripts/test-native-supervision.py`: expected output of the `virtual-tid` scenario.

## Testing

`test-launch.py` and `test-native-supervision.py` from this branch with `main`'s binary (2489517e, built from a clean tree) fail at the new `virtual-tid` case, 3 of 3 runs each; with this change both pass.

| case | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| `set_tid_address(&word)` in `launch` and `native` | `<host tid>` | `4242` |
| `getpid` / `gettid` in both lanes | `4242` / `-38` | `4242` / `-38` |
| `FUTEX_LOCK_PI_PRIVATE` on a zeroed word in both lanes | `0`, word `<host tid>` | `-1`, word `0` |
| same with flag bit 1024 | `0`, word `<host tid>` | `-1`, word `0` |

A dynamically linked glibc probe (manual run, not committed) in both lanes:

| glibc mutex | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| error-checking: `__owner` after lock | `<host tid>` | `4242` |
| `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`: lock word after lock | `<host tid>` | `4242` |
| robust: lock word after lock | `<host tid>` | `4242` |
| robust + `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`: lock word after lock | `<host tid>` | `4242` |
| return values of init / lock / relock or trylock / unlock | `0` / `0` / `35` or `16` / `0` | unchanged |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build` | pass |
| `make test-launch`, `make test-native-supervision`, `make test-gate1-setup` | pass |
| `make test-process-native` (lane unchanged), twice | pass |
| merged with #207 and #213: `git merge-tree` clean; `make check`, `make test-unit`, `test-launch`, `test-native-supervision`, `test-process-native` | pass |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

title: launch/native: set_tid_address and PI futexes expose the host tid next to the virtual pid
body:
## Summary

In `ginux launch` and `ginux native`, `getpid` is emulated and returns the virtual pid 4242, but the workload can still read its host tid in two ways:

- `set_tid_address` (218) is in the balanced task surface and executes on the host for its clear-on-exit registration (`decide_balanced` in `crates/ginux-core/src/lib.rs`, `Action::Mediate` arm of `supervise_launch` in `crates/ginux-init/src/launch.rs` and of `supervise_native` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`). Its return value is the caller's tid, and the exit stop passes it through unchanged. glibc stores this value as the thread's own tid during startup and later writes it into mutexes from userspace.
- `futex` (202) is mediated for every operation. `FUTEX_LOCK_PI` on a free futex word stores the caller's host tid in that word (likewise `FUTEX_LOCK_PI2` and `FUTEX_TRYLOCK_PI`), and `FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI` and the requeue-PI operations compare the word against it.

Neither lane creates a pid namespace, so the value is the tid the host sees: in a check run it was the supervisor's pid plus one, the forked tracee.

`ginux process-native` is not affected: it translates the `set_tid_address` result to the virtual tid at the exit stop and returns `-ENOSYS` for the PI futex operations (`supervise_process_native`, arms `SYS_SET_TID_ADDRESS` and `SYS_FUTEX`; `crates/ginux-init/src/process_hooks.rs`: "PI operations are denied because they expose host tids").

The other tid paths of these lanes do not leak: `gettid` (186) returns `-ENOSYS`, `clone` is denied, so `CLONE_PARENT_SETTID`/`CLONE_CHILD_SETTID` never write a tid, and the clear-on-exit write stores 0, not a tid.

## Expected

The workload sees one identity: `set_tid_address` returns the same virtual id as `getpid` (each lane runs one task without threads, so its tid is its pid), and no operation stores or compares the host tid in workload memory.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds a `virtual-tid` scenario to `tests/fixtures/launch-fixture.c` and `tests/fixtures/native-fixture.c`. It calls `set_tid_address`, `getpid` and `gettid`, then `FUTEX_LOCK_PI | FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG` on a zeroed static word and the same with one more flag bit (1024) on a second word, and prints each result and the words afterwards. With the PR checked out and `main`'s binary (2489517e) built from a clean tree, as root:

```
make build-launch-fixture
python3 scripts/test-launch.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/launch/launch-fixture
python3 scripts/test-native-supervision.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/launch/native-fixture
```

`test-launch.py` fails at `['virtual-tid']` with this workload output (3 of 3 runs):

```
set_tid_address=<host tid>
getpid=4242
gettid=-38
futex_lock_pi=0
pi_word=<host tid>
futex_lock_pi_flags=0
pi_flags_word=<host tid>
```

`test-native-supervision.py` fails at `thread identity is virtual` with the same values (3 of 3 runs); the audit shows the calls executed on the host:

```
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=3 phase=entry syscall=218 action=mediate surface=task result=pending
GINUX_FIXTURE: set_tid_address=<host tid>
GINUX_FIXTURE: getpid=4242
GINUX_FIXTURE: gettid=-38
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=9 phase=entry syscall=202 action=mediate surface=task result=pending
GINUX_FIXTURE: futex_lock_pi=0
GINUX_FIXTURE: pi_word=<host tid>
GINUX_NATIVE_AUDIT: sequence=12 phase=entry syscall=202 action=mediate surface=task result=pending
GINUX_FIXTURE: futex_lock_pi_flags=0
GINUX_FIXTURE: pi_flags_word=<host tid>
```

The same happens with an ordinary glibc program. A dynamically linked probe that locks an error-checking, a `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT`, a robust and a robust PI mutex reads the host tid back from each of them, in both lanes (the uncontended locks take glibc's userspace fast path, no syscall):

```
getpid=4242
errorcheck lock=0 owner=<host tid> relock=35 unlock=0
pi setprotocol=0 init=0 lock=0 word=<host tid> trylock=16 unlock=0 after=0
robust init=0 lock=0 word=<host tid> unlock=0
robust-pi init=0 lock=0 word=<host tid> unlock=0
```

## Suggested fix

- Keep `set_tid_address` mediated (the host still performs the registration), but replace its result at the exit stop with the balanced virtual pid, as `process-native` does with its virtual tid.
- Reject the PI futex operations (`FUTEX_LOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_UNLOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_TRYLOCK_PI`, `FUTEX_WAIT_REQUEUE_PI`, `FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE_PI`, `FUTEX_LOCK_PI2`) in `balanced_arguments_allowed`, so both lanes deny them through their existing argument check. Classifying the command by the low 7 bits of the operation word, as `process-native` does, covers every combination of flag bits, including the additional flag bits newer kernels accept.

A PR follows.

title: fix(process): deliver SIGINT/SIGTERM to a task parked in wait4
body:
Fixes #212

## Summary

- A blocking `wait4` with nothing reportable parks the caller at its entry stop. A managed SIGINT or SIGTERM to such a task executed on the host, but a ptrace-stopped task never dequeues a signal (only SIGKILL ends the stop), so the target never died and its parent's wait hung the domain.
- After a successful managed SIGINT or SIGTERM, every parked waiter of the target thread group is resumed with the new `wait_restart` flag. Its exit stop moves `rip` back over the two-byte `syscall` and restores `rax` to `wait4`; the arguments stayed untouched while parked. On the way back to user space the pending signal is delivered: with the default action the existing forwarding of fatal default signals kills the task and the parent's wait reports it; an ignored signal is dropped by the kernel and the restarted `wait4` parks again, as the wait keeps blocking on Linux.
- A `wait4` entry whose task already has a signal queued that is not blocked (`PTRACE_GETSIGMASK`) and whose default action terminates it (`PTRACE_PEEKSIGINFO`, private and shared queue) restarts the same way instead of parking. This covers a `kill` that executes before the supervisor handles the target's `wait4` entry stop. A blocked signal does not count, so it cannot restart the call forever; if the mask cannot be read, the wait parks as before.
- Always restarting is correct only because no handler can exist in this lane (`rt_sigaction` is `-ENOSYS`); with a handler Linux returns `-EINTR` unless `SA_RESTART` is set. The `wait_restart` comment records this.
- SIGKILL, parked waiters woken by a child state change and tasks that are not parked behave as before.
- Not covered: signals from outside the domain (sent by the host directly to a task, not through the managed `kill`), and signal numbers the managed `kill` does not forward (they still return `-ENOSYS`).

Details and reproduction: #212.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`: `NativeProcessTask::wait_restart`; `interrupt_parked_waiters`, called at the exit stop of a successful managed `kill` with SIGINT or SIGTERM; `termination_pending` (queued, unblocked, terminating by default), checked before parking; the restart in the exit stop.
- `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c`: scenario `parked_term` (a middle task parks in `wait4` for a grandchild, the root sends it SIGTERM and waits for it).
- `scripts/test-process-native.py`: expected lines for `parked_term`, 20 repetitions like the other race-prone scenarios.
- `Makefile`: `parked_term` added to `build-process-fixtures`.

## Testing

`scripts/test-process-native.py ... parked_term` with `main`'s binary (24a95402) fails with `process scenario parked_term hung`; run directly under `timeout 10`, 3 of 3 runs end with exit 124 after `wait parked caller=2` and `parked term kill=0`. With this change the scenario passes 20 of 20 runs in each of two full runs, and 50 of 50 direct runs.

| case | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| `kill(middle, SIGTERM)` while middle is parked in `wait4` | `0`, then hang | `0`, `wait interrupted caller=2`, `terminating signal=15`, parent `wait4` returns 2 with status 15 |
| same with SIGINT (fixture variant, not committed) | hang | parent `wait4` returns 2 with status 2 |
| `kill` immediately after the ready byte, no yield (fixture variant, not committed), 40 runs | not run | 40 of 40 pass; in this one timing-dependent sample 22 runs took the park-time path (`wait interrupted` without `wait parked`) |
| SIGTERM ignored by the launcher (`SIG_IGN` inherited), manual run | hang | middle task re-parks (`wait parked caller=2` again) and the wait keeps blocking, as on Linux |
| SIGTERM blocked by the launcher (mask inherited; the workload cannot change its mask, `rt_sigprocmask` is `-ENOSYS`), manual probe | hang | one `wait interrupted caller=2`, then the middle task re-parks quietly (no CPU use) and the wait keeps blocking, as on Linux |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build` | pass |
| `make test-process-native` (all scenarios incl. `parked_term` and `legacy`), twice | pass |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

title: process: SIGTERM to a task parked in a blocking wait4 is never delivered
body:
## Summary

In `ginux process-native`, a blocking `wait4` with nothing reportable parks the caller at its syscall-entry stop: the supervisor sets `orig_rax` to -1 and does not resume the task until a matching child state change wakes it (`supervise_process_native` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`, arm `61`, and `wake_waiters_for_child`). A managed `kill(pid, SIGTERM)` or `kill(pid, SIGINT)` executes on the host with the pid translated (arm `62`), so the signal is queued for the target. If the target is such a parked waiter, the signal is never delivered: a ptrace-stopped task does not dequeue signals, and only SIGKILL ends a ptrace stop by itself. The supervisor resumes the waiter only for a child state change. The `kill` returns 0, the target stays parked, and a parent waiting for it blocks forever, so the domain hangs.

The same happens when the signal is already queued at the moment the supervisor parks the waiter (the `kill` executes while the target's `wait4` entry stop is not yet handled).

SIGKILL is not affected (it ends the stop), and neither are tasks that are not parked: they take the signal at their next return to user space, where the existing forwarding of fatal default signals applies.

## Expected

As on Linux, the signal interrupts the wait: with the default action the target dies by it and its parent's `wait4` reports the signal (status 15 for SIGTERM). An ignored signal (`SIG_IGN` inherited across exec) leaves the wait blocking.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds the `parked_term` scenario to `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c` and `scripts/test-process-native.py`. The root forks a middle task, which forks a grandchild that blocks reading a pipe whose last write end the middle task holds. The middle task tells the root it is ready over a second pipe and calls `wait4` for the grandchild, which parks it. The root sends it SIGTERM and waits for it, expecting status 15. With the PR checked out and `main`'s binary (24a95402) built in a separate tree:

```
make build build-process-fixtures
python3 scripts/test-process-native.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/process target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/process-native-fixture parked_term
```

It fails with `RuntimeError: process scenario parked_term hung` (15 s timeout). Running the binary directly under `timeout 10` ends with exit 124 in 3 of 3 runs. Output of one run (host pids elided):

```
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS: virtual-init=1 host-pid=unexposed ptrace=attached
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: pipe task=1 read=3 write=4 cloexec=0
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: fork variant=fork host-result=... virtual-result=2
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: pipe task=2 read=5 write=6 cloexec=0
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: newborn-stop=deferred
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: newborn-stop=registered
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: fork variant=fork host-result=... virtual-result=3
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: close task=3 fd=6
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: close task=2 fd=5
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait parked caller=2 selector=3
parked term kill=0
GINUX_NATIVE_PROCESS_AUDIT: wait parked caller=1 selector=2
```

The `kill` succeeds, but no `terminating signal=15` line follows: task 2 stays parked, so task 1 stays parked waiting for it.

## Suggested fix

- After a successful managed SIGINT or SIGTERM, resume every waiter of the target thread group that is parked, with a flag that its exit stop restarts the call: `rip` back over the two-byte `syscall` and `rax` restored to `wait4`. On the way back to user space the pending signal is delivered and the existing forwarding of fatal default signals kills the task. An ignored signal is dropped by the kernel, the restarted `wait4` reaches its entry stop again and parks as before.
- Before parking, check with `PTRACE_PEEKSIGINFO` (private and shared queue) whether a signal that is not blocked (`PTRACE_GETSIGMASK`) and has a terminating default action is already queued; if so, restart the call the same way instead of parking.

A PR follows.

title: fix(init): kill the gate1 payload when ptrace setup fails
body:
Fixes #210

## Summary

- `supervise` (Gate 1) reported a `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` failure with `fail`, which exits the supervisor. `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` is not in effect yet, so the exit detached the payload from its stop after `execve` and it ran on untraced. A new `supervise_setup_fail` kills the payload with `kill(2)` and `SIGKILL`, reaps it and then calls `fail`, as `launch_fail` does in `launch.rs` (`native_fail` kills and reaps before reporting in the same way). It uses `kill(2)` rather than `PTRACE_KILL` because a policy that refuses the ptrace setup may refuse `PTRACE_KILL` too; the reap would then block while the payload stays stopped. Output and exit status stay the same (`GATE1: FAIL: PTRACE_SETOPTIONS failed`, exit 1).
- The `PTRACE_SYSEMU` failure right after it takes the same route. There `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` already kills the payload on exit, so this is only for consistency; its check passes on `main` too.
- The failure does not occur on an ordinary host (see #210), so the regression test forces it with a seccomp filter on the supervisor.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`: `supervise_setup_fail`, used by both setup failures in `supervise`.
- `tests/fixtures/gate1-setup-fixture.c`: freestanding x86-64 programs, built twice: `deny-ptrace <request> <program>` (seccomp filter that fails one ptrace request with `EPERM`, then `execve`; `all` fails every request except `PTRACE_TRACEME`) and a payload that creates `/var/tmp/gate1-payload-ran`.
- `scripts/test-gate1-setup.py`: runs `ginux` under `deny-ptrace` in a private mount namespace with a temporary directory bound over `/var/tmp`, for `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS`, `PTRACE_SYSEMU` and every request but `PTRACE_TRACEME`; requires exit 1 within 10 seconds, the matching `GATE1: FAIL` line and no marker within 2 seconds. The host's `/var/tmp` is not touched.
- `Makefile` (`build-gate1-fixture`, `test-gate1-setup`), `.github/workflows/check.yml` (`build-gate1-fixture` in the existing build step, `sudo make test-gate1-setup` in `launch-integration`), `README.md` (Linux integration steps), `docs/gate-1-foundation.md` (short paragraph under "Automated and human verification").

## Testing

`scripts/test-gate1-setup.py` with `main`'s binary (21e48f7c) fails its first check in 10 of 10 runs (`setoptions failure kills payload: exit=1 payload-ran=True`, output in #210); run on their own, the deny-all check fails the same way and the `PTRACE_SYSEMU` check passes. A variant of this change with `PTRACE_KILL` instead of `kill(2)` hangs in the deny-all case (`exit=timeout payload-ran=True`). With this change all three checks pass in 10 of 10 runs.

| scenario | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` fails | `GATE1: FAIL: PTRACE_SETOPTIONS failed`, exit 1, payload runs afterwards | same output and exit status, payload killed before it runs |
| `PTRACE_SYSEMU` fails | `GATE1: FAIL: PTRACE_SYSEMU unavailable`, exit 1, payload killed by `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` | same, payload killed and reaped before the exit |
| every request but `PTRACE_TRACEME` fails | `GATE1: FAIL: PTRACE_SETOPTIONS failed`, exit 1, payload runs afterwards | same output and exit status, payload killed before it runs |
| Gate 1 with `managed-payload`, no filter | `GATE1: PASS` | `GATE1: PASS` |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build`, `make test-process-native` | pass |
| `make test-launch`, `make build-gate1-fixture` and `make test-gate1-setup` as root on x86-64 Linux | pass |
| `make host-boot-test` and `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

The change does not overlap with #204 (native loop): `git merge-tree` of both branches is clean, and `make check` and `make test-gate1-setup` pass on the merged tree.

title: gate1: payload runs on untraced when PTRACE_SETOPTIONS fails
body:
## Summary

`supervise` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs` (Gate 1, `ginux` without arguments) waits for the payload's stop after `execve` and then sets `PTRACE_O_TRACESYSGOOD | PTRACE_O_EXITKILL`. If `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` fails, it calls `fail(b"PTRACE_SETOPTIONS failed")`, which prints `GATE1: FAIL` and exits the supervisor. At that point `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` is not in effect, so the exit detaches the payload instead of killing it: it leaves its stop and keeps running on the host, untraced and reparented. That contradicts the Gate 1 threat model in `docs/gate-1-foundation.md` ("traced from its first instruction after `execve`").

The other loops already kill and reap the tracee before reporting: `native_fail` (used by `supervise_native` and `supervise_process_native` for their `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` failures) and `launch_fail` in `launch.rs`, which uses `kill(2)` with `SIGKILL`.

The `PTRACE_SYSEMU` failure right after it is not affected: `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` is already set there, and the exit kills the payload (checked below).

## Scope

This is an error path. On an ordinary x86-64 Linux host I could not make `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` fail without help: the payload has just reported its stop, both options have been supported for a long time, and as far as I can tell no LSM hook sees requests on an already attached tracee (Yama and the LSMs check the attach, here `PTRACE_TRACEME`). The ways it can still fail are a seccomp policy around the supervisor that rejects this ptrace request, or a payload killed from outside between the wait and the call (then it is gone anyway). The documented Rocky setup does not hit it, and with the shipped `managed-payload` an untraced run only exits with status 1 (its emulated `getpid` check fails), so Gate 1 still reports `FAIL`. The point is that the supervisor should not leave a stopped, untrusted payload running on a failure path.

## Expected

On a setup failure before `PTRACE_O_EXITKILL` is in effect, the supervisor kills and reaps the payload before it reports `GATE1: FAIL`, as `native_fail` does.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds `tests/fixtures/gate1-setup-fixture.c`, built twice by `make build-gate1-fixture`:

- `deny-ptrace <request> <program>` installs a seccomp filter that fails `ptrace(<request>, ...)` with `EPERM` and executes `<program>`; `deny-ptrace all <program>` fails every request except `PTRACE_TRACEME`. The filter is inherited by Gate 1's tracee, which only uses `PTRACE_TRACEME`, so only the supervisor's request fails.
- `payload` creates `/var/tmp/gate1-payload-ran` when it runs.

`scripts/test-gate1-setup.py` binds a temporary directory over `/var/tmp` in a private mount namespace, installs `payload` there as `ginux-managed-payload`, runs `deny-ptrace <request> ginux`, and requires exit status 1, the expected `GATE1: FAIL` line, and that the marker does not appear within 2 seconds. With the PR checked out, build `main`'s binary (21e48f7c) in a separate tree, then run as root on x86-64 Linux (a user namespace with root mapped is enough):

```
make build-gate1-fixture
python3 scripts/test-gate1-setup.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/gate1/deny-ptrace .artifacts/gate1/payload
```

With `main`'s binary the first check fails in every run (10 of 10):

```
RuntimeError: setoptions failure kills payload: exit=1 payload-ran=True
GINUX: interception platform=ptrace-sysemu
GATE1: FAIL: PTRACE_SETOPTIONS failed
```

The supervisor reports the failure and exits, and the payload runs afterwards. Run on their own, the third check (every request but `PTRACE_TRACEME` denied) fails the same way (`exit=1 payload-ran=True`), and the `PTRACE_SYSEMU` check passes (`PASS gate1 sysemu failure kills payload`).

## Suggested fix

In `supervise`, kill and reap the payload before `fail` when `PTRACE_SETOPTIONS` fails. Use `kill(2)` with `SIGKILL`, as `launch_fail` does, not `PTRACE_KILL`: a policy that refuses the ptrace setup may refuse `PTRACE_KILL` as well, and the reap would then block while the payload stays stopped. The `PTRACE_SYSEMU` failure can take the same route for consistency.

A PR follows.

title: fix(scripts): verify cached Rocky domain rootfs hashes before reuse
body:
Fixes #208

## Summary

`prepare-rocky-domain.sh` now reuses the prepared domain cache only if the cached manifest and rootfs tar still hash to the `MANIFEST_SHA256` and `ROOTFS_SHA256` values it recorded in the metadata. On a mismatch it prints

```
cached <file> does not match <KEY> in <metadata file>; preparing again
```

to stderr and prepares again from the verified source QCOW2, the same path it already takes when the source or helper image changes. An unchanged cache is still reused, and with `GINUX_IMAGE_FORCE=1` the reuse check is still skipped, so the cached files are not hashed.

Intended behaviour change: `make test-image` (and `make demo-gate-2`) now repairs a modified cached manifest or tar in its initial prepare step, before its checks. Before, the run failed silently at [5/8] (modified manifest) or at [2/8]/[3/8] (empty tar, changed identity), or passed [2/8]..[5/8] on a modified tar that still contained the checked entries.

Details, consumers and reproduction: #208.

## Why re-prepare instead of failing

The source QCOW2 is verified against the pinned checksum in the same run, so preparing again restores the cache to a state that matches its metadata without a manual `make image-cache-clean`. This matches how the script already treats a stale `SOURCE_SHA256` or `HELPER_IMAGE`. The message makes the mismatch visible instead of silently re-extracting.

## Cost

Only the reuse path changes: one SHA-256 pass over the manifest and, if that matches, over the rootfs tar. That path already hashes the 545 MB source QCOW2 twice (`verify-rocky-host.sh` and `SOURCE_SHA256`). Fresh preparation is unchanged; it already hashes both files to record them.

## Changes

- `scripts/prepare-rocky-domain.sh`: add `cached_artifact_matches KEY FILE`, which compares `KEY=<sha256 of FILE>` with the metadata and reports a mismatch; append it for `MANIFEST_SHA256` and `ROOTFS_SHA256` to the reuse condition, after the existing checks.

## Testing

Sandbox: `prepare-rocky-domain.sh`, `rocky-domain-common.sh`, `verify-rocky-host.sh` and `config/rocky-domain-image.env` copied from the tree under test; a small fake host image with matching env and `.CHECKSUM`, so the real `verify-rocky-host.sh` passes; `qemu-img` stubbed to create the raw file; `docker` stubbed to succeed on `image inspect` and to write a small rootfs tar (`NAME="Rocky Linux"` in `./usr/lib/os-release`) and manifest on `run`, counting extractions. Cases run in sequence on the same cache.

| case | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| empty cache | prepared (1 extraction) | same |
| unchanged cache | "already prepared" (0 extractions) | same |
| cached tar replaced by one with `NAME="Modified"` | **"already prepared"**, cache keeps `NAME="Modified"` | `ROOTFS_SHA256` mismatch reported, prepared again, `NAME="Rocky Linux"` |
| cached manifest modified | **"already prepared"**, modified manifest kept | `MANIFEST_SHA256` mismatch reported, prepared again |
| cached tar truncated to 0 bytes | **"already prepared"**, empty tar kept | `ROOTFS_SHA256` mismatch reported, prepared again |
| `ROOTFS_SHA256` line removed from metadata | **"already prepared"** | `ROOTFS_SHA256` mismatch reported, prepared again |

All runs exit 0 on both trees. Sandbox only; a run against the real source QCOW2 and helper image with a modified cached tar was not performed.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `sh -n`, `bash --posix -n` on `scripts/prepare-rocky-domain.sh` | pass |
| `make check` | pass |
| `make test-image` with real artifacts (Docker, pinned helper image, verified source QCOW2) | not run for this change |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

title: scripts: `prepare-rocky-domain.sh` records rootfs and manifest hashes but reuses the cache without checking them
body:
## Summary

`scripts/prepare-rocky-domain.sh` writes `ROOTFS_SHA256` and `MANIFEST_SHA256` into the domain metadata (`rocky-10.2-x86_64-rootfs.env`) after extraction. Its reuse check, which decides whether to print "Rocky domain userspace already prepared" and exit, compares only:

- that the rootfs tar, manifest and metadata files exist,
- the manifest version line,
- `SOURCE_SHA256` against the freshly hashed source QCOW2,
- `HELPER_IMAGE` against the pinned helper image.

Neither recorded artifact hash is compared with the cached files in this reuse check, and no script reads `ROOTFS_SHA256`. A rootfs tar or manifest that was modified, truncated or replaced after preparation is reused without a message. The integrity record is written but not enforced.

Consumers of the prepared domain rootfs on `main` (0e06a986):

| consumer | what it does with the cache |
|---|---|
| `make image-prepare` (`prepare-rocky-domain.sh`) | reuse decision above |
| `make test-image` (`test-rocky-domain.sh`, part of `make test`) | runs `prepare-rocky-domain.sh`, then checks steps [2/8]..[5/8] on the cached tar and manifest; [5/8] compares `MANIFEST_SHA256`, nothing compares `ROOTFS_SHA256`. [6/8] then re-prepares with `GINUX_IMAGE_FORCE=1`, which overwrites the cache. |
| `make demo-gate-2` (`demo-gate-2.sh`) | runs `test-rocky-domain.sh`, then prints the identity from the cached tar |

So a modified manifest is caught later by `make test-image` [5/8] (the script exits through `set -e` without a message), while a rootfs tar that was modified but still contains the checked entries (non-empty, the required paths, Rocky 10.2 `os-release`, x86-64 `systemd`) passes [2/8]..[5/8] and is inspected as if it were the prepared one; only the forced re-preparation in [6/8] replaces it. `make image-prepare` alone keeps it. The OCI path (`prepare-rocky-oci.sh`) also records `ROOTFS_SHA256`, but it reassembles on every run and has no reuse path, so it is not affected.

## Reproduction

Sandbox on `main` (0e06a986): `prepare-rocky-domain.sh`, `rocky-domain-common.sh`, `verify-rocky-host.sh` and `config/rocky-domain-image.env` copied unchanged; a small fake host image with matching `config/rocky-host-image.env` and `.CHECKSUM` so the real `verify-rocky-host.sh` passes; `qemu-img` stubbed to create the raw file; `docker` stubbed so that `image inspect` succeeds and `run` writes a small rootfs tar (`./usr/lib/os-release` with `NAME="Rocky Linux"`) and a manifest, and counts the extraction. The cases run in sequence on the same cache.

| case | extractions | result |
|---|---|---|
| empty cache | 1 | prepared |
| unchanged cache | 0 | "already prepared" |
| cached tar replaced by one with `NAME="Modified"` | 0 | **"already prepared"**, cache keeps `NAME="Modified"` |
| cached manifest modified | 0 | **"already prepared"**, modified manifest kept |
| cached tar truncated to 0 bytes | 0 | **"already prepared"**, empty tar kept |
| `ROOTFS_SHA256` line removed from metadata | 0 | **"already prepared"** |

All runs exit 0.

## Suggested fix

In the reuse condition, also require that the cached manifest and rootfs tar still hash to `MANIFEST_SHA256` and `ROOTFS_SHA256` from the metadata. On mismatch, print which file did not match and fall through to the normal preparation from the verified source QCOW2, the same recovery the script already uses when the source or helper image changes. Checking the small manifest first and the tar last keeps the extra hashing to the case where every cheaper check has already passed.

Cost: the reuse path already hashes the 545 MB source QCOW2 twice (`verify-rocky-host.sh` and `SOURCE_SHA256`). The check adds one SHA-256 pass over the manifest and the tar on that path only; fresh preparation is unchanged, since it already hashes both to record them. `test-rocky-domain.sh` reads the whole tar again anyway (`tar -tf` and two `tar -xOf`).

A PR follows.

title: feat(console): support bounded polling of standard descriptors
body:
Programs using `poll` to wait for standard input or output readiness currently receive a policy denial in native execution. This adds a bounded allowance for descriptors 0–2 (plus ignored negative entries), with at most 16 entries and a timeout of 0–300 seconds. The supervisor validates the descriptor array before continuation; other descriptors, unreadable arrays, and unbounded waits remain denied.

Based directly on `main` at `0e06a986`. The launch fixture covers readiness, timeout limits, invalid pointers, descriptor restrictions, and closed descriptors.

Validation passed: `make check`, `make test-unit` (54 tests), release build, `test-launch`, `test-native-supervision`, and `test-process-native`.

title: fix(process): keep the stdio write rule for descriptor aliases
body:
Fixes #205

## Summary

- `FdEntry` gets an `origin` field: the stdio number (0, 1 or 2) an `FdKind::External` alias names. `PipeSpace::duplicate` sets it from the source descriptor and copies it for chained duplication; fork, `CLONE_FILES` and exec keep it with the rest of the entry. Pipe ends use 0.
- The process-native write arm applies the rule of that origin to an `External` alias: `-ENOSYS` for an alias of 0, the 4096-byte bound for an alias of 1 or 2. Before, every tracked descriptor executed on the host, so an alias of 0 wrote to the file behind the launcher's stdin although `write(0)` is denied, and an alias of 1 or 2 bypassed the bound. Pipe ends, plain stdio and untracked descriptors behave as before (`-EBADF` stays for untracked numbers above 2).
- `write` is the only write-like syscall this lane executes; `writev`, `pwrite64`, `sendfile`, `splice` and the others stay `-ENOSYS`, so no other path needs the check.

Details and reproduction: #205.

## Changes

- `crates/ginux-process/src/lib.rs`: `FdEntry::origin`, set in `create_pipe` and `duplicate`; unit test `stdio_aliases_keep_their_origin` (chained dup, `dup2(0, 1)` and back, fork inheritance, pipe end over 0).
- `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`: write arm of `supervise_process_native` decides by the origin of an `External` alias.
- `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c`: scenario `alias_writes` (plain stdin and stdout, `dup`, chained `dup`, `dup2`, `dup3`, `F_DUPFD`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`, `dup2(0, 1)`, short and 4097-byte writes through a stdout alias, the restored descriptor 1 and a stderr alias).
- `scripts/test-process-native.py`: expected lines for `alias_writes`; the scenario runs with an empty writable file as stdin, which must stay empty.
- `Makefile`: `alias_writes` added to `build-process-fixtures`.

## Testing

`scripts/test-process-native.py ... alias_writes` with `main`'s binary (0e06a986) fails with `scenario alias_writes wrote to the host stdin` (seven writes, output in #205). With this change it passes and the stdin file stays empty.

| write | `main` | this change |
|---|---|---|
| `write(0)`, `write(1)` with 4097 bytes | `-38`, `-38` | unchanged |
| through `dup(0)`, `dup(dup(0))`, `dup2(0, 7)`, `dup3(0, 8, O_CLOEXEC)`, `F_DUPFD`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC` of 0 | bytes written to the host stdin file | `-38` each, stdin file empty |
| `write(1)` after `dup2(0, 1)` | bytes written to the host stdin file | `-38` |
| through `dup(1)` and `dup(2)`, 16 bytes each | `16`, `16` | `16`, `16` |
| through `dup(1)`, and `write(1)` after `dup2(dup(1), 1)`, 4097 bytes each | `4097`, `4097` | `-38`, `-38` |
| through `dup(2)`, 4097 bytes | `4097` | `-38` |

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check`, `make check` (incl. clippy), `make test-unit`, `make build` | pass |
| `make test-process-native` (all scenarios incl. `alias_writes` and `legacy`), twice | pass |
| `make test` (Rocky host VM suite, QEMU TCG, macOS arm64) | pass |

title: process: descriptor aliases of stdio bypass the process-native write rule
body:
## Summary

In `ginux process-native`, `write(0)` is denied with `-ENOSYS` and writes to descriptors 1 and 2 are bounded at 4096 bytes (`supervise_process_native` in `crates/ginux-init/src/main.rs`, arm `1`). A descriptor created from stdio by `dup`, `dup2`, `dup3` or `fcntl` `F_DUPFD`/`F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC` is recorded in `PipeSpace` as an `FdKind::External` alias (`PipeSpace::duplicate` in `crates/ginux-process/src/lib.rs`). The write arm lets every descriptor that `PipeSpace::lookup` knows execute on the host without further checks, and `FdEntry` does not record which stdio descriptor an alias names. As a result:

- A write through any alias of descriptor 0 executes on the host and reaches the file behind the launcher's stdin, although `write(0)` itself is denied.
- `dup2(0, 1)` makes descriptor 1 such an alias, so `write(1)` reaches the same file.
- A write through an alias of descriptor 1 or 2 is not bounded at 4096 bytes. This includes descriptor 1 itself after `dup2(<alias of 1>, 1)`.

`write` is the only write-like syscall this lane executes; `writev`, `pwrite64`, `sendfile`, `splice` and the others stay `-ENOSYS` and are not affected. Reads are not affected either: reads from stdio are allowed for 0, 1 and 2 alike.

## Expected

An alias keeps the write rule of the stdio descriptor it names: writes through an alias of 0 return `-ENOSYS` like `write(0)`, and writes through an alias of 1 or 2 keep the 4096-byte bound (`-ENOSYS` above it). Pipe ends and plain stdio behave as now.

## Reproduction

The PR below adds the `alias_writes` scenario to `tests/fixtures/process-review-fixture.c` and `scripts/test-process-native.py`. The harness runs it with an empty, writable temporary file as stdin and fails if that file is no longer empty afterwards. With the PR checked out and `main`'s binary (0e06a986) built in a separate tree:

```
make build build-process-fixtures
python3 scripts/test-process-native.py <main>/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/ginux .artifacts/process target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/process-native-fixture alias_writes
```

It fails with `scenario alias_writes wrote to the host stdin: b'via-dup\nvia-dup-dup\nvia-dup2\nvia-dup3\nvia-dupfd\nvia-dupfd-cloexec\nvia-1\n'`. Excerpt of the workload output with `main`'s binary (audit lines, status lines and the written payload omitted; the 4097-byte writes are NUL bytes):

```
plain stdin write=-38
plain stdout write 4097=-38
dup stdin write=8
dup alias write=12
dup2 stdin write=9
dup3 stdin write=9
fcntl dupfd stdin write=10
fcntl dupfd-cloexec stdin write=18
stdin over stdout write=6
stdout alias write=16
stdout alias write 4097=4097
restored stdout write 4097=4097
stderr alias write=16
stderr alias write 4097=4097
GATE7_NATIVE_PROCESS: PASS
```

Every alias write except the short stdout and stderr alias writes should have returned `-38`; each of the stdin alias writes landed in the stdin file.

## Suggested fix

- `FdEntry` records the stdio number an `External` alias names (`origin`), copied on chained duplication and kept across fork and exec like the other fields.
- The write arm applies the rule of that origin to an `External` alias, and the existing rules to pipe ends and untracked descriptors.

A PR follows.

title: feat(process): supervise native processes with managed ownership
body:
human: Implementation planned by GPT-6.1 Sol high - implemented and PR submitted by muse spark 1.3 max - reviewed and fixed by GPT-6 astra high. The app [recipe](https://github.com/LevitateOS/recipe) is a package manager where an AI is the maintainer, Ginux provides the sandbox that recipe was missing for a long time.

## Summary
Extend the existing `process-native` fixture command with managed fork, clone, vfork, exec, threads, waits, termination signals, and pipes.

## Why
Native process events need consistent virtual identities and descriptor ownership, including child-first stops, worker-thread exec, and concurrent waits.

## Changes
Track process and descriptor lifetimes, translate identities and wait results, and reject unsupported syscall forms. Add native regression scenarios to Linux CI while preserving the existing unit suite.

## Testing
Formatting, Clippy, all 44 unit tests, all 19 native process scenarios, and configured-launch checks pass locally. Concurrency scenarios run repeatedly with varied CPU affinities. Full Rocky VM scenarios were not rerun.

## Notes
Based on upstream main. The command runs trusted host fixtures as the caller, without chroot; it does not enable children in configured `launch` or provide a general-purpose sandbox. General libc compatibility, signal handlers/job control, file and memory mediation, and PI futex operations remain unsupported.

title: feat(init): add configured native launch with faithful completion
body:
human: Implementation planned by GPT-6.1 Sol high - implemented and PR submitted by muse spark 1.3 max - reviewed and fixed by GPT-6 astra high. The app [recipe](https://github.com/LevitateOS/recipe) is a package manager where an AI is the maintainer, Ginux provides the sandbox that recipe was missing for a long time.

## Summary
Add `ginux launch <config> <root> [--result-file <fresh path>]` to execute a configured native workload with separate stdout and supervisor diagnostics, and report its actual exit code or terminating signal.

## Why
Native execution needs a reusable configuration-driven entry point and an authoritative completion record. Malformed commands, bootstrap failures, result-file failures, and unsupported execution modes must fail explicitly.

## Changes
- Extract launch, supervision, and syscall-dispatch extension points from the demo entry points.
- Add optional `[domain].workdir` (default `/work`, including support for `/`), bounded argv/environment staging, and explicit balanced/ptrace-native validation.
- Reserve result files with O_EXCL before executing a workload; check writes, fsync, and close. Existing result files are preserved. Startup failures return 2; supervision/result failures return 1.
- Preserve workload exit codes and terminating signals, including SIGTRAP; cap audit output and prefix supervisor diagnostics on stderr.
- Close inherited descriptors above stderr, reject alternate syscall ABIs, and deny fork until child ownership is implemented. Unsupported job-control group stops fail without hanging.
- Fix formatting and Clippy failures, and keep the freestanding linker out of Linux host build scripts.
- Preserve the existing unit-test modules and focused test targets. The required `static-and-unit` job runs both `make check` and `make test-unit`; a separate Linux job exercises real launch workloads.

## Testing
- `make check` and all 44 existing unit tests (`make test-unit`) pass. GitHub CI passes on `d8b011be`, including unit and launch integration coverage.
- `make build build-launch-fixture` passes.
- `sudo make test-launch` passes using real native workloads in temporary chroots: exit codes, signals, arguments, environment, workdir, input limits, unsupported configuration, missing executable, unprivileged bootstrap, descriptor isolation, fork denial, alternate ABI rejection, bounded audit output, result collisions, closed stdout, and an actual result-write failure via RLIMIT_FSIZE.
- Existing config, process, kernel-views, and runtime CLI outputs match the previous PR binary; lifecycle startup and SIGTERM cleanup pass on both. Existing invalid configuration fixtures remain rejected.

## Notes
The launch bootstrap requires host privileges and Linux 5.9+ for close_range, then drops to UID/GID 1000. Only stdio is inherited. Storage/device assignments, networking, resource quota enforcement, native child processes, subsequent exec, and retained-storage generations are outside this launch implementation. `generation` remains null. Config normalization now includes workdir. The complete Rocky VM integration suite has not been rerun.
